title: Kit Carson County well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: Kit Carson County wells have a median depth of 235 ft and a median yield of 20 gpm. See local depth ranges, water levels, and drilling cost estimates.
h1: Water wells in Kit Carson County, Colorado
intro_html: Kit Carson County sits on the High Plains, with a lot of production from the Ogallala and other High Plains aquifers, plus some fractured bedrock. Well records here are good enough to get a realistic sense of how deep you will drill, what kind of yield is common, and what that usually costs. This page pulls together the state permit data for the whole county so you can sanity-check a driller’s bid or a seller’s claims before you commit to land or a house on a well.

sections.heading: How deep wells run in Kit Carson County
sections.html:
Based on thousands of records, a typical Kit Carson County well ends up around a 235 ft total depth, with the middle half between 174 and 283 ft. About 72% of reported wells fall between 100 and 300 ft, and another 19% are in the 300–600 ft range. Very shallow holes under 100 ft are only 8%, and there is essentially no local pattern of ultra-deep domestic wells, even though the deepest well on record hits 3,130 ft.

On these plains, depth is mainly driven by where you sit relative to the Ogallala and other High Plains aquifer sands versus deeper fractured bedrock. Expect most driller bids to assume something close to the 200–280 ft band unless your specific spot has known deeper irrigation or stock wells.

sections.heading: Well yield: how much water you usually get here
sections.html:
Yield numbers in Kit Carson County are generally favorable. The median reported pump yield is 20.0 gpm, with the middle half of wells between 15.0 and 334.2 gpm. Only 4% of wells come in between 1–5 gpm, and there are 0% reported under 1 gpm. A strong 83% of wells report 15+ gpm.

From a buyer’s standpoint, that means most properly sited and completed wells here can easily cover an exempt household supply and typical stock use. Irrigation wells are part of that high-yield group too, so do not expect every domestic well to hit irrigation numbers, but it is reassuring that low-yield completions are uncommon in this dataset. Still, check nearby permits in your immediate area before assuming you will see 20 gpm on your own parcel.

sections.heading: Water levels and long-term trend on the High Plains
sections.html:
Static water levels in Kit Carson County are usually below the 100 ft mark, with a median depth to water of about 160 ft and a middle half between 121 and 188 ft. That means many wells have a decent water column above the pump once drilled out to 200–280 ft.

Looking at decades of measurements, median water levels were around 148–159 ft in the 1950s–1960s, improved to about 146 ft in the 1970s, then dropped deeper to roughly 182 ft in the 2000s. The 2010s pulled back to about 165 ft, with the 2020s around 172 ft. That pattern suggests a modest long-term decline with some recovery, typical of the Ogallala and High Plains Aquifer under mixed domestic, stock, and irrigation pumping.

sections.heading: Who has been drilling here and when
sections.html:
The county has a long record of well construction, with 6,729 wells in the state database and 2,870 recorded as constructed. Drilling has stayed steady over time: permits climbed from 161 in the 1950s to peaks of 810 in the 2000s, then eased to 343 in the 2010s and 268 so far in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2026, so the system is very much active.

The main drillers on record are Schaal Drilling Co. (Schaal, Ruben T.) with 888 wells, Parrish Drilling (Parrish, Wayne) at 382, and Klassen Drilling (Klassen, Paul C) with 204. Uses are a mix of about 30% domestic/household, 42% stock, 37% irrigation, and 3% monitoring, which lines up with what you see around Burlington, Bethune, Stratton, Flagler, Vona, and Seibert.

sections.heading: What a new well is likely to cost in Kit Carson County
sections.html:
The ground here is mainly alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, so drillers usually price by the foot. The typical rate in Kit Carson County runs about $35–$55 per foot. At the county’s median depth of 235 ft, the drilled hole alone pencils out to roughly $8,200–$12,900.

Once you add casing, grout, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical, a finished domestic well at that depth usually lands around $14,200–$24,900. If nearby wells on your parcel are closer to the 300 ft end of the local range, use that in your budgeting. Irrigation wells set up for high flow will be more expensive because of larger pumps and power service, even at the same depth.

sections.heading: Risks to watch for: water quality, dry holes, and siting
sections.html:
Low-yield wells are not common in the county data, with 0% under 1 gpm, but that does not mean you can ignore siting. Bedrock zones and the edges of the Ogallala can still be hit-or-miss at the parcel scale. Always look up the exact permits around your lot, not just county averages.

On the quality side, there are 17 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles in the wider area. Before closing on land, plan on a full lab test panel on any existing well and confirm future well and septic locations give you good separation and room for a replacement system.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a lot in Kit Carson County
sections.html:
Going into a land deal here, treat the county numbers as guardrails, not a guarantee for your specific tract. A reasonable expectation is a well in the 174–283 ft depth band with about 20 gpm of yield, drawing from the Ogallala, High Plains Aquifer, or unnamed fractured bedrock, but always verify with nearby well logs.

Confirm there is a valid DWR well permit or a clear path to getting one, especially if you are depending on exempt household use. Check how close you are to any listed PFAS or cleanup sites and budget realistically using the $14,200–$24,900 finished-well range. In open plains counties like this, driveway access, power runs, and septic can match the well cost, so plan the whole package, not just the hole.

faq.q: How deep are water wells in Kit Carson County, Colorado?
faq.a: State records show a median well depth of about 235 ft in Kit Carson County, with the middle half of wells between 174 and 283 ft. Around 72% of reported wells fall in the 100–300 ft range and another 19% are between 300 and 600 ft. Only about 8% are under 100 ft, and there is no common pattern of extremely deep domestic wells in this county.

faq.q: What is a typical well yield in Kit Carson County?
faq.a: Reported yields are generally strong. The median pump yield is 20.0 gpm, and the middle half of wells produce between 15.0 and 334.2 gpm. About 83% of wells report 15+ gpm, while 4% fall in the 1–5 gpm range and 0% are under 1 gpm. That is usually plenty for household and stock use, though individual parcels can still vary, so check nearby well records.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Kit Carson County?
faq.a: With local drilling rates around $35–$55 per foot in alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, a median-depth 235 ft well costs about $8,200–$12,900 for the hole alone. A complete domestic setup with casing, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical typically runs roughly $14,200–$24,900 at that depth. Deeper or higher-capacity irrigation wells, or long utility runs, will add to that total.

faq.q: Is the groundwater level dropping in Kit Carson County?
faq.a: Static water levels show some long-term decline with ups and downs. Median depths to water were about 148–159 ft in the 1950s–1960s, improved to around 146 ft in the 1970s, then deepened to roughly 182 ft in the 2000s. The 2010s improved to about 165 ft, and the 2020s sit near 172 ft. That pattern suggests modest drawdown over time, typical of Ogallala and High Plains pumping areas.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Kit Carson County?
faq.a: Safety depends on the specific well. Countywide data show 17 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles in the broader area. Many private wells are fine, but you cannot assume. For any existing or planned domestic well, budget for a full laboratory test panel and confirm siting away from septic systems and known contamination sources.
